action_criteria.expected_evidence: Severe active and chronic denervation in cervical muscles, active denervation in thoracic paraspinals and lumbosacral muscles with fasciculations and mildly large MUPs, tongue fasciculations only; normal conduction velocities without conduction block; sensory studies normal.
action_criteria.label: EMG and nerve conduction studies of the bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions to document lower motor neuron involvement and exclude conduction block and neuropathy
action_criteria.rationale: EMG/NCS confirms lower motor neuron involvement beyond the clinically affected muscles and excludes the main treatable mimics: multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block, demyelinating or sensorimotor neuropathy and myopathy. Gold Coast 2020 accepts EMG evidence of lower motor neuron dysfunction, and Awaji 2008 counts fasciculation potentials as active denervation in muscles with chronic neurogenic change.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No mass, brainstem lesion, demyelinating lesion or infarct; subtle precentral low T2 signal in the arm region (supportive only).
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude structural, vascular, demyelinating, inflammatory or neoplastic causes of the upper motor neuron or bulbar signs
action_criteria.rationale: MRI does not confirm ALS. It excludes brain and brainstem lesions that can cause upper motor neuron or bulbar signs; corticospinal tract signal change, when present, is supportive only.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Mild C3-C7 spondylosis without canal or significant foraminal stenosis and without cord compression; normal cervical and thoracic cord signal.
action_criteria.label: Spine MRI of the cervical and thoracic cord, and of the lumbosacral spine when lower limb signs need it, to exclude compressive myelopathy, radiculopathy and other cord lesions
action_criteria.rationale: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy with radiculopathy is the commonest structural mimic of combined upper and lower motor neuron signs in the limbs. Spine MRI excludes it, but incidental spondylosis does not explain bulbar signs or denervation in other regions and must not delay the ALS work-up.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: CK 1120 U/L (6.4x ULN); androgen receptor CAG repeat 21 (normal); blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function, B12, folate, ESR and CRP normal.
action_criteria.label: Blood tests for treatable mimics and a pre-treatment baseline: full blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes and calcium, CK, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and folate, ESR and CRP; plus the androgen receptor CAG repeat
action_criteria.rationale: These tests exclude metabolic, endocrine, nutritional and inflammatory mimics and give the liver and blood-count baseline needed before riluzole; phenotype-specific tests are added only when the case raises that mimic: here the androgen receptor CAG repeat, because a man with symmetric, proximal-predominant arm wasting and a raised CK raises spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy (Kennedy disease).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 78% predicted and SNIP 68 cmH2O, both mildly reduced: inspiratory muscle weakness at baseline, without an AAN 2009 NIV marker.
action_criteria.label: Baseline respiratory function (FVC and SNIP, with MIP where available) to stage respiratory muscle involvement and plan monitoring and NIV
action_criteria.rationale: Respiratory function does not diagnose ALS. Once ALS is supported it stages respiratory muscle weakness, sets the baseline for 3-monthly monitoring and identifies patients who need early referral for NIV.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No pathogenic C9orf72 expansion and no pathogenic variant in SOD1, TARDBP, FUS or TBK1; a negative result does not exclude ALS.
action_criteria.label: ALS gene panel (C9orf72 repeat expansion; SOD1, TARDBP, FUS and TBK1) after pre-test genetic counselling, once the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment is complete
action_criteria.rationale: Genetic testing does not make the diagnosis. It is offered with counselling to people with ALS because a pathogenic variant changes counselling for relatives and may open gene-targeted treatment or trials.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No clinically significant interaction with lisinopril; avoid heavy alcohol use because riluzole can raise transaminases; baseline and scheduled transaminase monitoring.
action_criteria.label: Check riluzole against the current medicines, alcohol use and liver function before the first dose, once the diagnosis is established
action_criteria.rationale: Riluzole is metabolised by CYP1A2 and can raise liver transaminases, so the medicine list, alcohol use and baseline liver function are reviewed before treatment. No current medicine interacts with it; his moderate alcohol use is worth reviewing because riluzole can raise transaminases.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not treat ALS with corticosteroids, IVIG or plasma exchange: they have no benefit.
Do not wait for FVC to fall below 50% or for respiratory symptoms before referring for NIV assessment.

Do not refer for cervical spine surgery on the basis of the mild C3-C7 spondylotic changes: there is no cord compression, and they do not explain the denervation in the thoracic and lumbosacral regions.
required_recommendations: Make and explain the diagnosis of ALS by Gold Coast 2020 criteria: progressive bilateral upper limb weakness and wasting (flail-arm phenotype) with upper motor neuron signs (brisk knee jerks and bilateral extensor plantar responses) and lower motor neuron involvement in the cervical and lumbosacral regions on examination and EMG, with active denervation also in thoracic paraspinal muscles, with mimics excluded by MRI and blood tests; disclose it in a planned face-to-face discussion with the patient and family.

Refer to the respiratory/NIV service now because FVC (78% predicted) and SNIP (68 cmH2O) are already reduced; screen for orthopnoea and nocturnal hypoventilation with overnight oximetry or capnography, and repeat FVC and SNIP within 3 months.

Offer riluzole 50 mg twice daily. Measure liver transaminases before the first dose, monthly for 3 months, every 3 months for the rest of the first year and periodically thereafter; stop riluzole if ALT exceeds 5x the upper limit of normal, and ask the patient to report any febrile illness so that neutropenia can be excluded.

Refer to a specialist ALS multidisciplinary team (neurologist, specialist nurse, respiratory, speech and language therapy, dietetics, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and palliative care), reviewed about every 2 to 3 months, with an early, patient-paced discussion of advance care planning.
Offer genetic counselling and, if the patient wishes, ALS genetic testing, explaining the implications for relatives.

avoided_actions.rationale: ALS is a motor-neuron disease without cortical electrical signature; EEG has no diagnostic role and adds cost without benefit.
ECG is unrelated to motor neuron disease and not part of the standard ALS workup absent specific cardiac symptoms or pre-medication QTc checks.
Echocardiography is unrelated to ALS diagnosis; no indication absent comorbid cardiac disease.
Cardiac monitoring has no role in ALS diagnostic workup.
MRI is the standard structural study for ALS workup; head CT adds no diagnostic value and exposes the patient to ionizing radiation.
Amyloid PET has no role in ALS diagnosis (motor-neuron rather than amyloid pathology) and carries a high cost.
DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic integrity; it has no role in ALS, which spares the dopaminergic system.
FDG-PET has no established diagnostic role in ALS and adds substantial cost.

key_clinical_evidence: Gold Coast 2020: ALS needs progressive motor impairment with upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least one body region, or lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least two, after other diseases are excluded. Here: brisk knee jerks and bilateral extensor plantar responses with lower motor neuron involvement in the cervical and lumbosacral regions, with active denervation also in thoracic paraspinal muscles.
EMG lower motor neuron evidence is chronic neurogenic change with active denervation; by Awaji 2008 fasciculation potentials count as active denervation in a muscle with chronic neurogenic change.
Normal motor conduction velocities without conduction block argue against multifocal motor neuropathy, and normal sensory responses argue against a sensorimotor neuropathy or SBMA.

The flail-arm phenotype (brachial amyotrophic diplegia) is an ALS phenotype with symmetric, proximal-predominant lower motor neuron weakness and wasting of both arms and relative sparing of the legs and bulbar muscles; it usually progresses more slowly than classic ALS, and upper motor neuron signs in the legs do not exclude it.

CK 1120 U/L is 6.4x ULN, higher than usual in ALS: consider a myopathic contributor clinically, while the neurogenic EMG pattern with fasciculations and upper motor neuron signs argues against a primary myopathy.

FVC 78% predicted and SNIP 68 cmH2O are mildly reduced. AAN 2009 markers that prompt NIV discussion are orthopnoea, FVC below 50% predicted, SNIP below 40 cmH2O, MIP weaker than -60 cmH2O or abnormal overnight oximetry; NIV prolongs survival and improves quality of life (Bourke 2006).
Spondylotic changes are common at this age; they cannot explain denervation in thoracic paraspinal and lumbosacral muscles, and here they cause no cord compression.

findings.finding: Bilateral FDI, APB, deltoids, biceps, triceps: fibrillations +3, PSWs +3, fasciculation potentials complex. Large amplitude severely reduced recruitment MUPs. Profound active and chronic denervation in all cervical-innervated muscles tested. Cervical paraspinals bilateral: fibrillations +2.
Bilateral TA, vastus medialis: fasciculation potentials, mildly large MUPs. Sparse fibrillations; minimal involvement.
Tongue: fasciculation potentials only; no fibrillations. Bulbar involvement minimal.

Bilateral median and ulnar motor: CMAP amplitudes severely reduced (right median 1.2 mV, left median 0.8 mV); distal latencies and conduction velocities normal. Peroneal and tibial motor studies normal. No conduction block, including across the proximal arm segments, and no temporal dispersion.

specialized_test.impression: Severe active denervation (fibrillations +3, positive sharp waves +3) and chronic reinnervation (large amplitude MUPs, severely reduced recruitment) in all cervical-innervated muscles tested, with fibrillations in the cervical and thoracic paraspinals. Fasciculation potentials, mildly large MUPs and sparse fibrillations in lumbosacral muscles. Tongue: fasciculation potentials without fibrillations. Severely reduced median and ulnar CMAP amplitudes with normal distal latencies and conduction velocities; no conduction block. Sensory NCS normal. Findings indicate a cervical-predominant disorder of anterior horn cells with thoracic and lumbosacral involvement.

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. A is a 56-year-old construction supervisor with 12 months of progressive bilateral arm weakness and wasting. The onset was insidious: he noticed difficulty lifting heavy equipment bilaterally and attributed it to bilateral shoulder problems. Bilateral shoulder MRI was obtained and showed rotator cuff tendinopathy but no significant tearing, insufficient to explain his weakness.

Over 12 months, his arms have become profoundly weak and visibly wasted. He can no longer lift his arms above shoulder height, cannot open jars, and requires assistance with dressing. He has visible twitching in both arms. Strikingly, his legs have remained entirely normal and he has no gait difficulty, no leg weakness, no sensory symptoms, and no speech or swallowing problems.

His bilateral arm areflexia was attributed to the bilateral rotator cuff issues. His primary care physician referred him for neurological evaluation.
